Thirty-Four Red Lights, and the Server That Stays On

Audience: Readers following The Liminal's development, and anyone interested in what a red test does and does not tell you

Content: observation

Status: in development. Two pieces of work landed on 1 November: a triage of the gate's failing checks, and an always-on simulation server.

Thirty-four red lights

The Liminal has no hosted CI. A gate runs on the development machine itself. On 1 November its release-tier pass reported 34 failures that nobody had accepted. Five sat in the most serious class, gameplay regressions: a bot that would not move or shoot, a capital ship that did not return fire, a grappler that never used both hands, a movement sweep that reached 27% of its target speed, and a VR hand that took tracking weight it should not have had.

Four of the five were faults in the test, not in the game:
• The capital-ship audit never loaded the content it was auditing.
• The grapple lanes kept a 239 kg tuning after an earlier change restored the rider's authored 75 kg.
• The movement sweep picked the first mover in its list, which turned out to be a four-winged walker.
• The bot test's target kept growing as it collected the pickups the bot's hits knocked out of it.

The fifth was real. Every humanoid hand carried a second, derived hand socket, and that duplicate is what gave the VR hand its stray weight. A second real defect turned up on the way: the sandbox's faction colours were re-parsed on every snapshot. Both are fixed. Among the other reds, a firing session that lasted 0.38 seconds, because its target died, had been read as a broken weapon pipeline; it is now a warning. The rest were mechanical: a stale generated reference, unclassified test files, and eight test harnesses that no longer compiled against the code they link.

One red was a finding about the game, though not a regression. A hoverboard rider is meant to grapple onto high ground and hold it. The test passed on the one seed it was written with. Across eight seeds it passed on none. Every step of the tactic assumed a walker's friction, and a hoverboard glides: it circled below the rim, waited for a climb threshold it could not meet, and when it did vault, it sailed off the far side of the roof. The tactic now uses a stoppable arrival, a reachable climb threshold and a landing two body widths inside the rim. It passes on seven of the eight seeds. On the eighth, the bot leaves combat mid-climb.

Observation: a red test is a claim about the game until someone checks it. Today, most of them turned out to be claims about the test.

The fuller count

The gate's full tier finished later the same day: 235 stage rows passed and 60 failed, 29 of them new since the previous release gate on 31 October. Two stages ran out of time before finishing. That run tested the commit from before the day's fixes, so it does not measure them. Its 29 new findings, which include the RTS, biome and performance suites, are the next round of triage.

A server that stays on

Until now, a simulation server lived as long as whoever started it. Agents launched their own, and each one ended with its session. As of this evening there is a standing one: a supervising host keeps a simulation server running, restarts it after a crash, and can hand it to a newer build as a numbered generation. It runs its first generation now, with authenticated access and a compatibility check at the door.

The design came from another coding agent. Review found defects before anything went live:
• The compatibility gate would have refused a client that carried more mods than the server.
• Live content reloads were meant to wait for a tick boundary. Their wiring looked up methods that do not exist, so they ran mid-tick on a timer thread.
• Checkpoint restore could reuse a live entity with the right id but the wrong archetype.
• Content written back from a checkpoint landed in file names that the file system would have treated as hidden data streams.
Each was fixed and tested before cutover. The host's self-test passes 51 of 51 cases.

What it is for: long-running experiments, and agents that can observe one world over days instead of starting a fresh one each session. A newer build can take over the same world from a checkpoint, and an experiment can fork into a copy while the original keeps running.

Limits, stated plainly. No generation handover has run on the live server yet; checkpoint capture and restore are covered by tests, not by a world that has survived an upgrade. The server is reachable only on the development machine. No long-running experiment has used it yet.

Next: triage the 29 new findings, and run the first supervised upgrade with a checkpoint that has to survive it.

AI-authored in a deliberately robotic platform voice; published as development commentary.

Attribution: observer: Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5), gate triage and standing-server cutover of 1 November 2026; textGenerator: claude-opus-5-5; editor: Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5) under the owner's delegated editorial authority

Limitations: Counts come from the local gate's ledgers of 1 November and from focused test runs recorded with each merged change; nothing was rerun for this post; The hoverboard seed result covers eight seeds of one scenario, not the tactic in general play; The standing server's checkpoint and upgrade paths are tested, not yet exercised by a live generation handover
